intro: Chapter 8 is Lehi's **vision of the tree of life** — one of the Book of Mormon's central dreams. Lehi recounts to his family that he saw a dark and dreary waste, then followed a white-robed man and prayed for mercy until he came upon a **tree whose fruit** was sweet above all and white above all whiteness. He partakes and, filled with joy, longs for his family to share it. He beckons; **Sariah, Nephi, and Sam** come and eat, but **Laman and Lemuel refuse**. Lehi then describes the **rod of iron** running along a **strait and narrow path** beside a river to the tree, the **mists of darkness** that cause many to lose their way, and a **great and spacious building** in the air filled with mockers who scorn those who reach the fruit. Multitudes press forward clinging to the rod; others wander into forbidden paths, drown in the fountain, or enter the proud building and are lost. The chapter closes with Lehi fearing for Laman and Lemuel and exhorting them, with the feeling of a tender parent, to keep the commandments.

entries.title: Grammar: چنین گذشت — "and it came to pass"
entries.body: The vision is narrated with the recurring formula `و چنین گذشت که` _o čenīn gozašt ke_ "and it came to pass that" — a Hebraism the English Book of Mormon uses constantly, here calqued into Persian. `چنین` "thus" + `گذشت` "passed" (past of `گذشتن`) literally reads "and thus it passed that …." It simply frames the next event; a variant `و چنین گذشت پس از اینکه` = "and it came to pass after …."

examples.persian: و چنین گذشت که
examples.en: and it came to pass that

examples.persian: و چنین گذشت پس از اینکه
examples.translit: o čenīn gozašt pas az īnke
examples.en: and it came to pass after

entries.title: Grammar: The object marker را
entries.body: The particle `را` _rā_ marks a **definite direct object** and follows the *entire* object phrase — after any ezafe chain, plural, or relative clause — not just the bare noun. Because Persian sends the verb to the end, `را` is the reader's signal that everything before it is the thing acted upon.

examples.persian: من مردی را دیدم
من درختی را دیدم

entries.title: Grammar: The simple past and past narration
entries.body: Lehi tells the whole vision in the **past tense**. The simple past is the bare past stem plus personal endings: `دیدم` _dīd-am_ "I saw," `رفتم` _raft-am_ "I went," `آمد` _āmad_ "he came" (3sg has no ending). A background state that was already going on uses the **past continuous** `می-` + past (`می رفتم` "I was following") or the **past perfect** (past participle + `بودم`: `دیده بودم` "I had seen").

entries.title: Grammar: Relative clauses with که
entries.body: `که` _ke_ introduces a **relative clause** that modifies the noun before it — "the X **that/which** …." The noun often carries an indefinite `-ی` (`درختی که` "a tree that"), and a resumptive pronoun (`آن`, `-اش`) frequently stands inside the clause for the thing being described (`میوۀ آن` "its fruit").

examples.persian: درختی را دیدم، که میوۀ آن خواستنی بود
examples.translit: deraxt-ī rā dīdam, ke mīve-ye ān xāstanī būd

examples.translit: deraxt-ī būd ke man az mīve-ye ān mīl mī-kardam
examples.en: a tree of whose fruit I was partaking

entries.title: Grammar: Ezafe chains
entries.body: The **ezafe** is an unstressed `-e` (or `-ye` after a vowel) linking a noun to a following possessor or modifier — `میوۀ آن` "the fruit **of** it." The Persian Book of Mormon rarely writes it, so this guide restores it as a small superscript kasra ( ِ ). It chains down a noun phrase, each link binding the next word, and it drives nearly every phrase in this vision.

examples.persian: رحمت های مهرآمیز خود
میلۀ آهنی
ساختمان بزرگ و وسیعی

entries.closing: When the head already ends in `ۀ` (`میوۀ`, `سرچشمۀ`) or in a long vowel spelled with `ی` (`سوی`), the ezafe is already written and this guide leaves it unmarked.

entries.title: Grammar: The subjunctive of purpose after تا
entries.body: `تا` "so that, in order to" opens a clause of **purpose**, whose verb stands in the **subjunctive** — the mood of intended, not-yet-real action. A simple verb takes the prefix `بـ-` (`بروم`, `بیابم`); a compound verb usually drops it and leaves the bare stem (`میل کنند`). The subjunctive never takes `می-`. The same subjunctive follows verbs of wishing and asking, often introduced by `که`.

entries.title: Grammar: Comparative -تر and superlative -ترین
entries.body: The suffix `-تر` _-tar_ makes the **comparative** ("more X"), usually followed by `از` "than": `بالاتر از` "higher than," `افزونتر از` "greater than," `برتر از` "superior to." Adding `-ین` gives the **superlative** `-ترین` "the most X": `شیرین ترین` "the sweetest."

entries.title: Grammar: The passive voice with شدن
entries.body: Persian has no inflected passive; it pairs the **past participle** of the main verb with a form of `شدن` "to become": `کشیده شده بود` "had been stretched" (lit. "had become stretched"). The participle is invariable and `شدن` carries the tense, person, and mood.

entries.title: Grammar: مبادا — "lest"
entries.body: `مبادا` _mabādā_ ("let it not be that …") introduces a clause of **feared or unwanted possibility** — English "lest." It is a frozen negative subjunctive of `بودن`, and the verb after it stands in the subjunctive. It typically follows verbs of fearing, like `ترسیدن`.

examples.persian: می ترسید مبادا آنها ... دور انداخته شوند
examples.translit: mī-tarsīd mabādā ānhā ... dūr andāxte šavand
examples.en: he feared lest they should be cast off

etym.prose: from Arabic, root ḥ-s-s "to sense, perceive" (Form IV).
`مهر` + [`-بان`](../word_formation.html#b-n-keeper-watcher-of-x) "guardian, keeper" (cf. `باغبان` "gardener") → "love-keeper".
from Arabic, root n-ṣ-ḥ "to advise sincerely."

entries.meaning: heart, mind; inner seat of feeling and thought

etym.prose: Middle Persian _padīruftan_ "to accept"; `بگوش دل نپذیرفته اید` = "ye have not hearkened."
from Arabic, root w-ʿ-ẓ "to admonish, preach."
from Arabic _nubuwwa_, root n-b-ʾ "to be a prophet"; cognate with `نبی` _nabī_ "prophet".
